evidence: Sen. Ep. 6.1: nōn ēmendārī mē tantum sed trānsfigūrārī
Cic. Leg. 3.30 (Lewis & Short): tōta cīvitās ēmendārī et corrigī solet continentiā prīncipum
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “to free from faults, to correct, improve, amend”: a text, a habit, one’s own life. Traupman gives it for “improve” with an object. The verb meliōrāre is post-classical (Dig.).

evidence: Publ. P 62: Peccātum extenuat, quī celeriter corrigit.
terms.comment: Of putting right what is wrong; Lewis & Short: “to improve, amend, correct, make better, reform”.

terms.gloss: refine, cultivate (the mind, manners, a place)
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “to improve, ennoble, refine, perfect (the class. signif. of the word)”, as of minds trained by study.

evidence: Gell. 1.17.4 (Varro): quī fert, sēsē meliōrem facit
terms.comment: The plain phrase for making a person or a thing better.
Morgan–Owens’s rendering; for the passive, Seneca’s in melius mūtārī, see improve, get better.

phrases.latin: Intellegō, Lūcīlī, nōn ēmendārī mē tantum sed trānsfigūrārī.
phrases.english: I can see, Lucilius, that I am not just being improved but transformed.

phrases.latin: Ex vitiō alius sapiēns ēmendat suum.
phrases.english: From another’s fault the wise man corrects his own.

phrases.latin: vitium … uxōris aut tollendum aut ferendum est. quī tollit vitium, uxōrem commodiōrem praestat, quī fert, sēsē meliōrem facit
phrases.english: A wife’s fault must be either cured or borne: whoever cures it makes his wife easier to live with; whoever bears it makes himself better.

sources: Lewis & Short: emendo · Lewis & Short: corrigo · Lewis & Short: excolo · Lewis & Short: melior · Lewis & Short: muto
